commentBody: A Zhou Zheng puzzle? THATSMYJAM.
Thanks for trying your hand at a themeless, Zhou Zhang! This one was fun, and I was glad to see that I could solve it albeit slowly, through the fog of a tired brain.

Loved it!  My solve started fast, slowed way down, then sped back up, finishing just barely below my average time.  But the creativity was the main thing.  

As soon as I saw the clue for 17 Across, I started wondering, "How daring will this get?"  Just the right amount, was of course the answer.  Also loved "etch" crossing "itch."

After a couple of days where I was not inspired by the puzzles, my spirits were lifted to see a Zhou Zhang offering for Friday.  And a righteous Friday it was.  IMEANCOMEON! It took me so long to get a foothold that I thought my brain would GOSPLAT (great clue and answer btw).  In fact it was GOSPLAT that broke the puzzle open for me.  The key to this puzzle was uniformly excellent cluing and a variety of fun entries.

And, to top it off, I got a trip down memory lane thinking about all the late night television watching I did in my youth, and all the commercials for GINSU knives that I suffered through as a result.

I’d love to CONFABULATE with y’all, but my brain needs a rest.
Whew! That was fun and challenging. Felt like a good Friday puzzle (no pun intended).

Congrats Zhou!
I know from experience how hard it is to construct a good themeless (still unsuccessful). I hope everyone else understands that this is a much more difficult skill than a themed puzzle and not every constructor can make the transition. This one was quite  challenging for a Friday and sparkled. Not surprised that you pushed yourself to do it, nor the quality of the work, and hope to see you finish the cycle soon!

The scholarly jury is out on whether William of Ockham ever uttered the parsimonious phrase associated with his name. The "razor" is simply a term applied to any thesis whose point is to shave off alternative and less worthy solutions. There are other razors:

Hanlon's razor: Never attribute to malice that which can be adequately explained by stupidity.

Alder's razor: If something cannot be settled by experiment or observation, then it is not worthy of debate. (Obviously Alder was no fun at parties, or even at lunch). 

Hitchen's razor: That which can be asserted without evidence can be dismissed without evidence.

John Ezra's Razor: If you call someting a Natick you will live to regret it.

If the kilocalorie is now a capital C calorie then someone should let NIST know. Units that derive their name from a person are lower case when written out in full but upper case in their abbreviation. A ampere, W weber, K kelvin …. All units are lower case when written out. The upper Celsius is because it’s always preceded by a lower case degrees. https://www.nist.gov/pml/special-publication-330/sp-330-section-5#5.2 Also the primary language for units is French.

It's funny how a wrong answer with a right letter can accidentally unlock things for you. I do question ANECDOTE being clued by "recollection", though.  It really depends on who's doing the recollecting, doesn't it?  When your conversational mate is an amusing and witty type, every recollection will be an ANECDOTE and you'll be spellbound.  But when your conversational mate turns out to be a bore, every recollection will be drawn-out and dreary and you'll want to get away as fast as your little feet will carry you.

(I do have someone in particular in mind.)

I’m still trying to decide whether NORMIE is pejorative. The context in which I hear that word these days is in reference to people who pay less attention to current political news than you and the person you’re talking to. Thus remarks like “I think it’s a scandal, but the NORMIEs will have forgotten it tomorrow if they notice it at all.” I think it often includes a note of jealousy over the ability not to obsess, and so almost a degree of admiration as well as condescension.

By the way, I thoroughly enjoyed the puzzle too, but I finished in less than half my average time, and therefore thought I would open the comments and find nothing but remarks about too easy, too easy, too easy. It just goes to show you how different we can be.
Here I am again asking for Fridays (and Saturdays) to be more difficult. This was a fine puzzle and all, but it felt like a Wednesday.

Picture me half an hour later about to GO LOCO, poised like a SAMURAI brandishing GINSU knives, and shouting “UNFAIR!” at my seemingly perfect fill. In such a conundrum, one usually SNIFFS OUT the problem eventually (with a few OMS), but after coming up BARREN for the UMPTEENTH time, I accepted my NORMIE solver status and used my web-browsing APP to relieve the metaphorical ITCH. My mom died suddenly in April from a fall in her nursing home. I am still lost.

Mom had been on a 5 year spiral into vascular dementia set off by a dissected aortic aneurysm (TAAA) in the early months of COVID. Her illness taught me to appreciate a different definition of CONFABULATE. 

Merriam-Webster says “Confabulate is a fabulous word for making fantastic fabrications.”  

Telling a completely believable stories about the cruise she never took and how her toothbrush ending up in her purse — and she clearly thought she was telling the truth — but IMEANCOMEON. Her storytelling was our first sign of what was to come, and also hilarious. 

Thanks for a reason to make me smile, Zhou Zhang.

At least the clue - or the answer - should remain in English. E.g.: the answer to the 15 across clue "Dios mío!" is correctly answered as "Aycaramba!".

From Google/AI:

"¡Ay, caramba!" is a Spanish exclamation used to express surprise, shock, excitement, or mild annoyance. It is similar to saying "Oh my gosh!", "Oh boy!", or "Good grief!" in English. 

Spanish clue "Dios mío!" leading to Spanish exclamation  "Aycaramba". Really?

Additionally, as Cheri point out below, confabulate does not mean “shoot the breeze”. Cheri quotes Merriam-Webster:

“Confabulate is a fabulous word for making fantastic fabrications.”

Two unforced errors, IMHO.

Can't imagine having any kind of a chance at that one. Here's the link: https://www.xwordinfo.com/Crossword?date=3/29/2001&h=20a ....

Thanks for the challenging but fun puzzle. Just wanted to say that CONFABULATE has a much more specific definition than "shoot the breeze." It means "to make up stuff," as Alzheimer's patients tend to do. A fabulist is someone who makes up (often unbelievable) stories. When we shoot the breeze, we don't usually make up crazy stories - at least the people I know don't.

@Matt

 To start with, on the most obvious basis, themeless puzzles are expected to have a lower word count. Themed puzzles generally have a 72-78 word count and themeless, 72 or less. So it’s much harder to have good fill. Then, as CCNY indicated, having a good theme does most of the work for you. The theme may suggest a few fresh entries and the rest can be pretty standard and come from a standard wordlist. Also the grid shape is suggested by the theme requirements. 

For themeless, you really need at least a few long, original entries you can’t get from the standard wordlists or the software. Often people will start with a fresh seed entry or two that excited them. The best solvers, I think, collect interesting phrases and add them to their word lists. And, of course, balancing trivia and proper nouns with other exciting words and phrases that are more accessible.

And then, of course, the challenge of clueing the whole thing cleverly so that there is enough of a challenge (clearly a difficult task for your standards lately) but not completely out of reach and finding clues to clue the more obvious glue (because there always is some).

It’s an entirely different experience for a constructor and quite daunting.
You were right the first time.  A themeless should have better fill, because theme answers have little or no flexibility, and there's a sort of domino effect on the non-themers.
